Antipsychotic Adverse Effects

acute dystonia · akathisia · parkinsonism · tardive dyskinesia · neuroleptic malignant syndrome · metabolic and prolactin effectsWhich effect, timed from the start or the last dose increase, and what is the next step?

1Script2Urgent3Differential4Workup5Criteria6Severity7Treatment8Follow-upPractice
1Drug script
Bottom line
  • Clock it from the start or last increase: dystonia hours to days, akathisia and parkinsonism weeks, tardive dyskinesia months to years
  • Fever, lead-pipe rigidity and confusion building over days mean neuroleptic malignant syndrome (NMS): stop the drug, then cool and give fluids
  • Clozapine: check the ANC (absolute neutrophil count) before and during treatment; clozapine, InjectionOlanzapine also comes as a long-acting injection, used less because each injection needs an observation period for delirium and sedation. and quetiapine carry the most metabolic harm; screen weight, glucose and blood pressure at least yearly
What it is

Dopamine receptor blockers: antipsychotics antiemetics such as metoclopramide and prochlorperazine

Mechanism

Dopamine D2 receptors blocked antipsychotic effect

Blockade in the striatum acetylcholine outweighs dopamine dystonia and parkinsonism

Anticholinergic balance restored dystonia usually eases within minutes

Used for

Psychosis: second-generation drugs favored first line

Clozapine: schizophrenia after 2 or more failed adequate trials, or with increased risk of suicide or aggression

Acute mania severe agitation in delirium

Huntington disease: may partly suppress Huntington diseaseA VMAT2 (vesicular monoamine transporter 2) inhibitor is typically first line for chorea; avoid it with depression.

Risks

NMS laryngeal dystonia clozapine: severe neutropenia, myocarditis, seizures

Movement: dystonia, akathisia, parkinsonism, tardive dyskinesia

Metabolic (clozapine, olanzapine, quetiapine) prolactin (first-generation, risperidone) QTc (QT interval corrected for heart rate) prolongation, most with thioridazine and ziprasidone; torsades de pointes with haloperidol

Insights

Every class can cause NMS, second generation included switching drugs is no safeguard

Anticholinergics relieve dystonia and parkinsonism, but may worsen tardive dyskinesia, so stop them there

Adverse effects, by time coursedetail behind the risks
HoursAcute dystonia, usually within hours to days of the first dose; an emergency department antiemetic can do itlaryngeal spasm can stop breathing
DaysNMS builds over 1 to 3 days, usually after a start or dose increase (the main risk factor) but possible at any timerisk highest with high-potency or depot drugs, several antipsychotics together, or added lithium
WeeksAkathisia, the most common extrapyramidal effect, typically within 4 weeks (overall range hours to months); parkinsonism within days to weeks, tremor often on both sides
Months to yearsTardive dyskinesia after prolonged use, more than 6 months; about 10% to 20% after a year of treatmentorofacial forms are commonest
After stoppingWithdrawal-emergent dyskinesia after an abrupt stop, more common in children; clears in 4 to 12 weeks
ClozapineAgranulocytosis in just under 1%, usually within 3 months; the risk never reaches zeroseizures dose dependent, about 1% to 6%; drooling (sialorrhea); constipation that can progress to ileus
By potencyExtrapyramidal riskAmong second-generation drugs, risperidone carries the highest extrapyramidal risk; quetiapine and clozapine the lowest. High-potency first-generation drugs (eg haloperidol), more so at higher doses, drive extrapyramidal effects; low-potency drugs and clozapine are the most anticholinergic and sedatingseizures too are commonest with low-potency drugs and clozapine, especially at high doses
Who is at riskHigher-potency drugs, higher doses, prior extrapyramidal effects; young men for dystonia, older women for parkinsonism and tardive dyskinesia
2Urgent risks
NMSFever, rigidity, confusion and unstable vital signs on a dopamine blocker
CK (creatine kinase) can be very ↑ and typically tracks severity Guideline detailLeukocytosis, myoglobin in the urine, falling kidney function. Most often high-potency first-generation (eg haloperidol), but any class, olanzapine included

If NMS is suspected, choose stopping the antipsychotic, then cooling and fluids.

AirwayDystonia of the larynx or pharynx

If breathing is threatened, choose airway assessment and an intravenous anticholinergic.

ClozapineSevere neutropenia; also myocarditis, cardiomyopathy, seizures, profound hypotension
ANC before starting and throughout treatment Agranulocytosis usually within 3 months Myocarditis mostly in the first 4 weeks, at any dose

If the baseline ANC is <1500/µL, choose not starting clozapine (initiation is not recommended).

DementiaOlder adults with dementia-related psychosis
Boxed warning, first- and second-generation alike: Boxed warningDeath risk about 1.6 to 1.7 times higher, with more stroke and heart attack.
3Differential
Which effect is it, most tempting first
Effect or mimicFingerprintDecides it
Acute dystoniaNamed formsNamed forms: oculogyric crisis (eyes forced upward), torticollis (painful neck twist). of neck, jaw, eyes or tongue; mind clear; antiemetics such as metoclopramide can cause itWithin hours to days of a start or increase; half by 48 hours, 90% by day 5
AkathisiaAkathisiaAripiprazole is commonly linked to it. (in dementia, akathisia may contribute to agitation)Typically within 4 weeks of a start or increase (overall range hours to months); the restlessness is felt from within
Drug-induced parkinsonismTremor, rigidity, slow movement, masked face, shuffling gaitDays to a few weeks; tremor often symmetric; reversible
Tardive dyskinesiaLip smacking, tongue darting, cheek puffing, jaw movementsMonths to years of treatment, usually past 6 months
Neuroleptic malignant syndromeFever, lead-pipe rigidity, confusion, autonomic instability, ↑ CKUsually after a start or increase (the main risk factor), but possible at any time; builds over 1 to 3 days; no clonus
HypocalcemiaFacial muscle spasmParesthesia, hyperreflexia and a cause such as neck surgery
Fever, agitation, clonus, hyperreflexia, vomiting or diarrheaWithin hours (under 24) of a serotonergic change; clonus, not rigidity
Malignant hyperthermiaFever and rigidity, as in NMSDuring or just after a volatile anesthetic or succinylcholine
CatatoniaLittle movement, unresponsive, posturingPlain catatonia does not explain fever or autonomic instability; the malignant form can, but shows posturing and waxy flexibility
Angioedema or anaphylaxisTongue pushed outSwelling, not spasm

Pause point. The bait: NMS offered as serotonin syndrome from a drug interaction, or as malignant hyperthermia, and dystonia offered as hypocalcemia or as agitation needing more haloperidol. Rigidity and fever building over days on a dopamine blocker is NMS; a spasm within hours in an alert patient is dystonia, and an anticholinergic treats it.

7Treatment
Manage by effect
Effect or situationDoAvoid
Acute dystoniaA parenteral anticholinergic (benztropine or diphenhydramine); intravenous relief in about 3 to 5 minutes; intravenous benztropine is followed by an oral doseMore haloperidol: further blockade would likely worsen it
AkathisiaLower the dose, or stop the antipsychotic if the lower dose helps little; or switch (clozapine, olanzapine, quetiapine); propranolol if the dose must stayRaising the dose (akathisia is dose dependent); reaching first for a In dementiaIn dementia, benzodiazepines generally have no role: falls, dependence, paradoxical agitation. Memantine, a dementia drug, has no evidence for akathisia, and moving the patient to a nursing home is premature before a treatable drug cause is addressed. or benztropine (less favorable safety)
ParkinsonismLower the dose or switch to a second-generation drug; amantadine, or an anticholinergic short termAnticholinergics in older adults
Tardive dyskinesiaStop anticholinergics; valbenazine or deutetrabenazine if moderate to severe; stop the antipsychotic or switch (eg clozapine) if possibleAnticholinergics: they may worsen it
Neuroleptic malignant syndromeStop the antipsychotic, then cool and correct fluids and electrolytes (ladder below)Swapping in another antipsychotic: every class can cause it
Metabolic harmAlsoAlongside lifestyle measures, metformin can counter the weight gain.In practiceAn American Family Physician review places quetiapine one tier lower, in a middle group with less metabolic harm than the top three.
Parkinson disease or Lewy body dementia; see Quetiapine, pimavanserin or clozapineRisperidone, olanzapine, Guideline detailIn Lewy body dementia, typical drugs, even at very low doses, tend to worsen extrapyramidal signs.
High-risk patient (eg young man, prior dystonia) given an intramuscular first-generation drugGive diphenhydramine or benztropine with itWaiting for dystonia to appear before giving the anticholinergic
1

FirstNMS suspected

Stop the antipsychotic
2

Supportivethe antipsychotic is stopped

Aggressive cooling; correct volume deficits and electrolytes

Admit to an intensive care unit for close monitoring; a benzodiazepine may help agitation. Case reportsElectroconvulsive therapy (ECT) has been reported to work in refractory cases. Restarting after NMSThe recommended cautious rechallenge: wait at least 2 weeks after it resolves, then a lower-potency drug at a low dose with slow titration.

3

Optionsbeyond supportive care

Bromocriptine (a dopamine agonist) or dantrolene (a muscle relaxant)
8Follow-up
Monitoring
WhenCheckWhy
Every patientWeight, glucose and blood pressure at least yearly, with counseling against weight gainClozapine, olanzapine and quetiapine carry the most metabolic risk
Second-generation drug, from the startFasting glucose and lipids, weight and blood pressure Guideline detailWeight at baseline, 4, 8 and 12 weeks, then quarterly; glucose and blood pressure at baseline, 12 weeks, then yearly; lipids at baseline, 12 weeks, then every 5 years (adapted from the 2004 American Diabetes Association consensus).Metabolic harm
On clozapineANC before starting, weekly to month 6, every 2 weeks to month 12, then monthlySevere neutropenia, likeliest early, never zero
Starting haloperidol (eg, for delirium)Baseline ECG (electrocardiogram) for the QTc (rate-corrected QT interval)Haloperidol can cause torsades de pointes; QTc prolongation is most marked with thioridazine and ziprasidone. QTAmong second-generation drugs, ziprasidone and quetiapine carry the greatest QT risk.
Long-term useOrofacial movementsAbout 10% to 20% develop tardive dyskinesia after a year of treatment
AripiprazoleLow-dose aripiprazole can counter the prolactin rise through partial D2 agonism. Whether the patient takes a drug that commonly raises prolactin (any first-generation drug, risperidone)Dopamine D2 block in the tuberoinfundibular tract raises prolactin: galactorrhea, amenorrhea, gynecomastia, sexual dysfunction, bone loss
Interactions
WithEffectDo
Fluvoxamine or ciprofloxacin (inhibitors of cytochrome P450 1A2, CYP1A2)Clozapine levels riseCheck the level; watch for dose-dependent effects such as seizures
Tobacco smokingSmoke induces CYP1A2 and lowers clozapine levels; quitting raises themSmokingAfter quitting, the dose may need lowering: check the level and watch for seizures; after starting, watch for lost effect
Practice
  1. 23-year-old man given intramuscular haloperidol for agitation 8 hours ago now his neck is twisted to the right and his eyes are fixed upward Alert; speaks clearly; no stridor T 37.1 °C · HR 104/min · BP 138/84 mm Hg → Benztropine → acute dystonia within hours of a dopamine blocker: an anticholinergic such as benztropine gives rapid relief; dantrolene belongs to neuroleptic malignant syndrome and propranolol to akathisia
  2. 19-year-old woman in the emergency department for vomiting 1 hour after intravenous metoclopramide: jaw clenched, tongue pushing out, words slurred Fully alert; no lip or tongue swelling; no wheeze BP 118/74 mm Hg · HR 96/min → Diphenhydramine → an antiemetic dopamine blocker caused acute dystonia: a parenteral anticholinergic such as diphenhydramine usually works within 30 minutes; with no lip or tongue swelling this is spasm, not angioedema, so epinephrine is not needed, and nothing in the history points to hypocalcemia, so calcium gluconate has no role
  3. 34-year-old man started haloperidol 2 weeks ago for schizophrenia cannot sit through visits; paces, shifts his legs, says he feels driven to move voices quieter; dose cannot be lowered HR 82/min · no rigidity or tremor → Add propranolol → inner restlessness with a compelling urge to move within 4 weeks of starting is akathisia; propranolol treats it when the dose cannot be lowered; more haloperidol would worsen it, and valbenazine is for tardive dyskinesia
  4. 46-year-old woman whose risperidone dose was doubled 3 weeks ago both hands shake at rest; slower walking with short steps; blank face No lip smacking or tongue movements T 36.9 °C · cogwheel rigidity both arms · alert, oriented → Drug-induced parkinsonism → tremor, rigidity, slow shuffling gait and masked face within weeks of a dose increase; tardive dyskinesia comes months to years later with orofacial movements, and there is no fever or altered mental status
  5. 58-year-old man with schizophrenia on haloperidol for 9 years constant lip smacking and tongue darting that embarrass him and disrupt eating takes benztropine as well BP 128/80 mm Hg · no tremor or rigidity → Stop benztropine and start valbenazine → orofacial movements after years of a dopamine blocker are tardive dyskinesia; anticholinergics may worsen it and should be stopped, and moderate to severe disease is treated with a VMAT2 (vesicular monoamine transporter 2) inhibitor
  6. 52-year-old man started on risperidone for schizophrenia 6 days ago now disoriented, diaphoretic and rigid in all limbs T 40.3 °C · BP 172/100 mm Hg · HR 118/min · reflexes normal, no clonus · creatine kinase 24,000 U/L → Neuroleptic malignant syndrome → fever, rigidity, altered mental status, autonomic instability and a high CK developing over days, even from a second-generation drug; serotonin syndrome comes within hours with clonus and hyperreflexia; acute dystonia is a localized spasm of the neck, jaw, eyes or tongue
  7. 29-year-old woman started on haloperidol in hospital 4 days ago rigid, confused, febrile; creatine kinase rising No new serotonergic drugs T 39.8 °C · HR 120/min · BP 164/98 mm Hg · urine dark → Stop haloperidol; cool; give fluids → neuroleptic malignant syndrome: stopping the drug is paramount, then aggressive cooling and fluids; another antipsychotic can cause it too, an anticholinergic does not treat it, and bromocriptine or dantrolene are options beyond supportive care
  8. 32-year-old man with schizophrenia stable on olanzapine for 1 year gained 14 kg; new fasting glucose 128 mg/dL Wants to stay on an antipsychotic BMI (body mass index) 33 kg/m² · BP 136/86 mm Hg · triglycerides 260 mg/dL → Aripiprazole → metabolic harm is greatest with clozapine, olanzapine and quetiapine and lowest with aripiprazole, ziprasidone and lurasidone; screen weight, glucose and blood pressure at least yearly
  9. 27-year-old woman with schizophrenia on risperidone for 8 months no periods for 4 months; milky nipple discharge Urine pregnancy test negative; no headaches TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone) normal · BP 110/70 mm Hg · visual fields full → Dopamine blockade raising prolactin → risperidone, like any first-generation drug, commonly raises prolactin, causing amenorrhea and galactorrhea; a normal TSH argues against hypothyroidism, and with no headache and full visual fields nothing suggests the mass effect of a large adenoma, so the dopamine blocker she already takes is the likely cause
Pairs with SSRI Adverse Effects: hours after a serotonergic change, with clonus? Schizophrenia: Long-Term Care: relapsing on the antipsychotic, and which added psychosocial treatment answers it? Parkinson Disease and Parkinsonism: motor disease and parkinsonism mimics.
Transferable rule

Time the movement from the start or the last dose increase before naming it: hours to days is dystonia, weeks is akathisia or parkinsonism, months to years is tardive dyskinesia.
